title: NDIS blowouts lead $145b surge in surprise costs
full_text:
The Albanese government has faced $145 billion in spending blowouts since coming to office on the back of repeated cost overruns in major programs including the National Disability Insurance Scheme, fuelling economists' concerns that promises of budget restraint are falling short of reality.
The analysis, compiled by HSBC chief economist Paul Bloxham, comes amid mounting pressure for Treasurer Jim Chalmers to deliver sweeping cuts in the mid-year update in December to reduce inflation pressures.
Deloitte Access Economics partner Stephen Smith said the federal and state governments were making the inflation problem worse, even if they were not its main cause, and argued they should run balanced budgets over the course of the economic cycle.
"But it isn't the case right now. Australian governments are currently running expansionary fiscal policy even though the economy is - according to the Reserve Bank of Australia - operating above its potential level of activity," said Smith.
The Australian Financial Review reported on Tuesday that Chalmers would need to find about $11 billion in cuts at the mid-year budget update in December to offset the effect of surging government bond yields and the cost of backflips and delays to savings measures outlined in May.
These include reversing cuts to veterans' medical entitlements, lifting the refugee intake, delaying NDIS changes and uncertainty over savings from scrapping the higher private health insurance rebate for over-65s, which remains in legislative limbo.
Bloxham said there had been significant upside spending surprises at the past five updates, with unexpected revisions totalling $136.8 billion since May 2024. Over the life of the Albanese government, unexpected spending revisions totalled $145.6 billion.
The figures capture so-called "program-specific parameter variations", which measure changes in spending forecasts due to factors specific to individual programs, rather than new policy decisions. The cost overruns do not necessarily translate into actual spending, since the government can subsequently scale back a program to offset higher forecast costs.
The extra spending over the past few years reflects a combination of blowouts in new government policies and increases in the cost of demand-driven schemes such as JobSeeker, school funding and disaster relief.
Veteran budget watcher Chris Richardson said the public service was rapidly getting worse at forecasting the cost of government.
"You want the public service to be able to produce, on average, unbiased forecasts. Nobody demands or expects perfection, but we're talking huge dollars, so it's worth understanding if there's something systematic going on," Richardson said.
"To be fair, the economy grows over time. Yet, even as a share of the economy, recent errors are 24 times worse than their pre-COVID average, while the [December 2025 mid-year] update weighs in at a stonking 58 times worse."
The NDIS has consistently been the largest source of overruns. The May 2024 budget revealed a $15.9 billion blowout in projected spending on the scheme, while the May 2026 budget recorded another $13.9 billion uplift in forecast outlays, prompting the government to announce a major overhaul of the scheme.
The December 2025 mid-year update revealed an $11.6 billion overrun in forecast outlays on Energy Minister Chris Bowen's policy to subsidise household batteries, forcing the government to drastically rein in the scheme to claw back billions. The program was originally forecast to cost just $2.3 billion over four years.
Projected spending on aged care surged $13.4 billion at the May 2023 budget after the Fair Work Commission ordered a 15 per cent pay rise for 250,000 aged care workers - a decision strongly supported by the government and funded by taxpayers. Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said the spending variations were a normal feature of the budget process and driven by factors outside any government's control.
"Since 2022, we have had to accommodate significant parameter variations, including $40 billion in social security payments due to indexation and growing demand, $20 billion in additional natural disaster relief to the states, and $15.8 billion in additional veterans' payments as we have cleared the Coalition's claims backlog," Gallagher said.
Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson said NDIS corruption and abuse had long been reported, but the Albanese government had been dragged kicking and screaming to reform.
"Because the treasurer is addicted to spending, NDIS abuse has led to taking advantage of the most vulnerable, abused taxpayers' money and it's stoked inflation too," Wilson said.
The Parliamentary Budget Office in July warned the budget's forecasts were built on "systematic optimism", including banking savings from yet-to-be-legislated policies and relying on assumptions that inflated future revenue and understated spending.
The final budget outcome for 2025-26, released last month, showed real federal spending increased 4.3 per cent last financial year, more than double the projection of 1.8 per cent growth contained in the 2024-25 budget, prepared just two years earlier. The figures are adjusted for inflation.
Other than during the pandemic, spending has hit a four-decade high, a surge many economists argue had made the RBA's fight against inflation harder.
